name: West Ridge

waypoints.name: PCT North Trailhead, Snoqualmie Pass (I-90 Exit 52)
waypoints.note: Large paved lot just north of I-90 exit 52; $5 self-issue Northwest Forest Pass fee, then north on the PCT into Alpine Lakes Wilderness.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52 at Snoqualmie Pass. Cross under the freeway and take the first right; the PCT North (Commonwealth Basin) trailhead lot is a large paved lot on the right, at about 3,000 feet. Self-issue a Northwest Forest Pass ($5) at the trailhead before heading north on the Pacific Crest Trail into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

waypoints.name: Kendall Katwalk
waypoints.note: 150-yard path blasted into a steep granite cliff face on Kendall Peak's north ridge; narrow and exposed, can hold snow/ice into early July.

waypoints.name: Gravel Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water at the lake outlet; established sites only, no fires permitted above 4,000 ft in this basin.

waypoints.name: Ridge Lake
waypoints.note: Established PCT campsites on the far shore and on the slope down to Gravel Lake; last easy camp before the Bumblebee Pass turnoff, 0.4 mi ahead.

waypoints.name: Bumblebee Pass
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT here on a steep, poorly-marked climber's path up a short gully; easy to walk past in fog or low light.

waypoints.name: Bumblebee Basin
waypoints.note: Small scenic basin on the far side of the pass, standard bivy for the climb; only intermittent tarns for water, check conditions before relying on them.

waypoints.name: Crux 5.6 Roofs (Pitch 2)
waypoints.note: Pull over the route's technical crux here on otherwise solid rock; rope up for pitches 1-4 before easing off into the Class 3-4 traverse.

waypoints.name: Mount Thomson
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a final scramble over ledges and cracks (P6); descend the East Ridge with one to three rappels from established stations.

approach: Park at the PCT North (Commonwealth Basin) Trailhead lot just off the frontage road at Exit 52, Snoqualmie Pass (~3,000 ft) — cross under I-90, take the first right, and the lot is on the right. From the trailhead, follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; it climbs steadily through timber via long switchbacks for roughly 5.5–6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk (~5,400 ft), a narrow, exposed ledge blasted directly into the rock face of Kendall Peak's south side — solid underfoot but very exposed, use caution if icy or in high wind. Continue north on the PCT about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake (~5,260 ft), the last reliable water source and a common camp/rest stop (roughly 2–2.5 hrs / ~7 mi in from the car). About 0.4–0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching left (west) off the PCT; it climbs a steep ~200 ft to Bumblebee Pass (~5,400 ft), a small saddle above Alaska Lake. The path is loose and eroded in spots on both the up and down sides — take care with footing. Drop off the far side of the pass into Bumblebee Basin (scattered camps, seasonal water), then contour/ascend northwest across talus and scree (worse-looking than it climbs) toward the lowest notch on Thomson's west ridgeline (~5,960 ft). Short sections of 4th-class scrambling around a set of gendarmes lead to the notch at the base of the route, where the first pitch starts just left (north) of the crest. Total trailhead-to-base distance is about 8–8.5 miles with roughly 2,900–3,000 ft of gain, typically 4–5 hours for a fit party; most groups do the climb car-to-car in one long day, though the basin makes a fine camp for a two-day trip.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the basin, then the lowest notch on the west ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the PCT North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, about 3,000 ft: cross under I-90, take the first right, lot on the right. Follow the PCT northbound through timber on long switchbacks for roughly 5.5 to 6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk at about 5,400 ft, a narrow ledge blasted into the rock of Kendall Peak's south side — solid underfoot, very exposed, and worth care if icy or windy.

Continue north about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake at about 5,260 ft, the last reliable water and a common camp; roughly two to two and a half hours and about seven miles from the car.

About 0.4 to 0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching left (west) off the PCT. It climbs a steep 200 ft to Bumblebee Pass at about 5,400 ft, above Alaska Lake. Drop off the far side into Bumblebee Basin, then contour and climb northwest across talus and scree toward the ridge.

About 8 to 8.5 miles and 2,900 to 3,000 ft to the base, typically four to five hours for a fit party.
hazards: The Kendall Katwalk, exposed and dangerous when icy or windy
Loose and eroded tread on both sides of the Bumblebee Pass boot path
Talus and scree in the basin below the ridge
A descent by the East Ridge, meaning a route-finding descent on unfamiliar ground at the end of a long day
A long day: many parties climb it car to car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Aim for the lowest point in the ridge, and know in advance that it is further left than it looks. From Bumblebee Basin, scrambling up scree, the beginning of the ridge that you can see from below is not where you want to be. The notch you want is left of it, at the ridge's lowest point, around 5,960 ft. That single correction is the most useful thing on this approach, because the eye pulls you right every time.

The notch is small, and its size is the confirmation: it holds about three people at most. If you have topped out on a broad, comfortable saddle, you are not at the start of the West Ridge.

Expect short fourth-class scrambling around gendarmes to reach it. Once you top out on the ridge you scramble over a small gendarme, traversing rightward toward the crest, to gain the notch itself.

The first move settles it absolutely: pitch one begins with a step left into a well-featured chimney. That step-left-into-a-chimney is the signature of this route and is probably the crux of the whole climb. If your first pitch is a face or a slab, you are not in the right notch. The first two leads run up a series of chimneys in solid rock.

And the other route on this peak is on the opposite side: the East Ridge is class 3-4 and is gained from a notch at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side, from the same basin. If you are on easy scrambling ground the whole way, you are on the East Ridge and you have circled to the wrong end of the mountain.
